If a police officer is committing a crime during the investigation, is there any way the defense could ask that the actual evidence not be admissible? If so, is it likely that such a motion would be granted?

The question is always whether or not it is relevant to the case. It is a general rule that you aren't allowed to admit things which are unrelated to the case, but if something is probative to the facts of the case, it may be admissible.

The logs angle is probably what is important here - if a bunch of items were seized from a person's home and not recorded, then it is legitimate for them to argue that the logs of what was claimed to be taken from the home are untrustworthy. This is a chain of custody issue. However, the most likely argument from the defense standpoint would be even before the trial to argue that the chain of custody has been broken because the logs are unreliable and there's no way to prove that the evidence seized matches up with what was actually taken from the house because of the inconsistencies in the log, and therefore the evidence should be suppressed. This would likely ruin the prosecution's case. Even if they failed to get it suppressed, presenting evidence that the logs were tampered with or fraudulent may be enough to trigger "reasonable doubt" in the jury.

This is the sort of thing that is likely to be admissible in court - it calls the facts being presented into question, facts which directly pertain to guilt and innocence, and therefore is likely to be probative and relevant. It may be prejudicial in a sense, but it is hard to argue it is unfairly prejudicial because the chain of custody is so important.

On the other hand, a police officer stealing money from a wallet seems less likely to be relevant. That's outright criminal activity, but it has no particular bearing on the suspect's guilt or innocence as it relates to drug offenses. Does the officer stealing money from the suspect have anything to do with whether or not the individual was dealing drugs?

This is known as being probative - basically, the evidence in question needs to be relevant to the factual legal questions of the case. Being the victim of a crime doesn't have any relevance to whether or not you committed a crime yourself.

Another issue is whether or not the evidence in question is unfairly prejudicial - basically, "Oh, that officer is a criminal, therefore this person should walk." That's not a valid chain of legal logic, and the fact that so many people immediately jumped to it in this discussion is a good example of exactly why such evidence might be excluded - it has no bearing on the suspect's guilt or innocence, and is instead being used to play on people's emotions.

The states with the lowest homicide rates - in the northeastern and northern regions, as well as one in the Pacific - have wildly variable gun ownership rates, with the first three having high rates of gun ownership, and the Pacific state having the lowest in the country.

So-called petrodollar recycling is when a petroleum-exporting country spends petrodollars externally—essentially, a country selling oil would then either buy imports from other countries or invest money overseas rather than domestically. This occurs because they earn more money than they feel is profitable to invest in their own countries, leading them to invest abroad or purchase imports due to limited local production capabilities.

It has been common for certain oil-producing countries to invest significantly in a large economy and purchase many capital goods from it (this economy is a major exporter of capital goods, something many people may not realize). The Korean writing system is an alphabet and looks quite unique. If you look at the symbols, you'll see that what appear to be single signs are actually multiple independent, fairly simple signs arranged above, below, or beside each other. This is because the Korean writing system has consonants and vowels, similar to the Latin alphabet, and is written in blocks, each block consisting of 2-6 letters. Each block forms a single syllable.

It is a pretty cool way of writing.

Conversely, some other East Asian languages use logographic characters, so when you see something like a specific character, it is likely from one of those languages. These characters can be quite complex, but they don't have the same appearance of multiple distinct-but-simple characters arranged together.

One of those languages also has a phonetic script that looks somewhat like simplified logographic characters, and it doesn't have the distinctive block structure of the Korean writing system. This phonetic script represents syllables, while another phonetic script from the same language looks quite different and is frankly probably not easily distinguishable.

But you can definitely tell the difference between the Korean writing system and the logographic systems, as the Korean alphabet looks very different from those other writing systems.

Imagine you and your opponent both have a latency of 80 milliseconds. That's 5 frames at 60 frames per second.

Your opponent does something at time = 0 that eliminates you or prevents you from acting. You respond 1 frame later (so at time = 1 frame). At 5 frames in, the server receives the input from the other player indicating that they performed an action that affected you. The server will relay this information on its next update (so at 6 frames in) to inform you that you were hit and unable to act. At time = 11 frames, your device receives that message, and at time = 12 frames, it actually displays what "really" occurred.

That's 1/5th of a second, at minimum, where you are incapacitated but unaware of it. It could be even longer if there are additional delays due to random lag or other factors.

40 ping is more than two frames. Realistically speaking, you're probably looking at 3 frames from the other player to the server, at least 1 frame on the server, and 3 frames from the server to you, plus at least 1 frame on your end before you see what "really" happened.
